extracted.intended_audience: researchers/authors submitting manuscripts to Wellcome Open Research (and similar open peer review journals)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for authors on how to read, organise, implement, and respond to peer reviewer comments (within an open peer review / post-publication review model), and how to prepare a clear response letter and subsequent revisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand the open peer review model
rubrics_metrics.description: Wellcome Open Research uses an open peer review model, where reports are public, and the identities of authors and reviewers are known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Embrace transparency: it encourages constructive feedback, enhances accountability, acknowledges reviewers by publicising their names and reviews, can speed up publishing times and enhance research impact, and helps authors build trust in the feedback and confirm reviewer expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read all reviewer comments thoroughly and document requested revisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Once you receive the reviewer comments, take the time to read them thoroughly and understand them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List all the changes reviewers have requested by moving each suggestion into a new document; use line numbers or bullet points to separate feedback; include a separate section for comments from each reviewer so nothing is missed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorise each comment (four main categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: You can consider separating each comment into one of four main categories:
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The four categories are: (1) Valid and essential suggestions — clear issues or improvements that significantly enhance the work; (2) Comments that require clarification — reviewer misunderstandings or requests for more information that should be answered or clarified; (3) Comments that can be politely declined — suggestions that do not align with research goals or fall outside the study scope, where authors should explain rationale for not incorporating them; (4) Comments about minor revisions — small changes that do not affect conclusions (missing refs, data presentation, typos, phrasing). Use this classification to prioritise changes and structure responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Highlight edits in the manuscript and use track changes
rubrics_metrics.description: Start planning where you’ll make the changes and what those changes should be. Copying the reviewer’s feedback into comments within your manuscript can help locate edits and show how suggestions relate to each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Turn on 'track changes' to mark all changes so you can locate them later when writing your response letter; highlighting and inline comments make it easier to map reviewer suggestions to manuscript edits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarify points reviewers misunderstood rather than assuming they are wrong
rubrics_metrics.description: If reviewers point out aspects you believe have already been explained in your paper, do not assume they lack understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: View misunderstandings as opportunities to clarify: add sentences or references to explain the point further, because if one reviewer is confused others may be too. Ensure clarifications do not appear as though you ignored the feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decide carefully where changes cannot or should not be made and explain why
rubrics_metrics.description: You might decide not to revise your paper if it needs a lot more research or changes the focus of your work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Peer review is a discussion — it is acceptable to politely disagree with a reviewer if you have good reasons. For changes you cannot or will not make, explain this clearly in your response letter with rationale (e.g., out of scope, requires new data).

rubrics_metrics.name: Craft a clear, well-structured response letter
rubrics_metrics.description: Start your response document with a brief introduction, thanking the reviewers for their feedback. Organise your letter with clear headings for each reviewer’s comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quote the reviewers directly and briefly explain your responses; use examples and set revisions apart with italics or text boxes for emphasis. A response letter can be fairly long but should be clearly structured and formatted. Keep tone respectful and professional, thank reviewers for their time, and emphasise commitment to improving the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare for additional rounds of feedback
rubrics_metrics.description: After resubmitting to Wellcome Open Research, prepare for another round of peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers often ask for more revisions or clarifications after initial changes. Approach subsequent rounds with the same professionalism and commitment. Treat peer review as a collaborative effort to improve quality and impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organise responses per reviewer and make mapping between comment and change explicit
rubrics_metrics.description: Include a separate section for comments from each reviewer and map each comment to the change made (or the reason for not changing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoting reviewer comments and then responding directly, with references to manuscript locations (line/section numbers) or by showing tracked edits, makes it easy for reviewers and editors to verify how feedback was handled.
